before.content_html:
Overview

Blood Brothers has a relatively small cast of named characters, but each one plays a crucial role in exploring the play’s themes of class, fate, and nature versus nurture. All other characters are played by the ensemble. Understanding how each character develops from childhood to adulthood is essential for the exam.

Mickey Johnstone

Mickey is one of the twin brothers, raised by his biological mother Mrs Johnstone in a working-class household. As a child, he is energetic, cheeky, and streetwise. He looks up to his older brother Sammy and dreams of being tough like him. When he meets Edward at age seven, he is friendly and open despite their different backgrounds.

As an adult, Mickey’s life takes a very different path from Edward’s. He leaves school without qualifications, works in a factory, and faces unemployment when Mr Lyons makes his workforce redundant. After being pressured by Sammy into a robbery, Mickey is sentenced to seven years in prison. He comes out broken, dependent on antidepressants, and unable to be the husband Linda needs. His tragic decline represents how poverty and lack of opportunity can destroy a person.

Key Fact

Mickey’s key line is “I could have been him!” This reflects his growing envy of Edward’s privilege and is central to the theme of nature versus nurture. The same person, raised differently, could have had a completely different life.

Edward Lyons

Edward is Mickey’s twin, raised by the wealthy Lyons family. As a child, he is polite, well-spoken, and lonely. He uses an RP accent that reflects his privileged upbringing. When he meets Mickey, he is enthusiastic and sincere, saying “Do you want to be my friend?” with genuine excitement.

As an adult, Edward goes to university, becomes a city councillor, and enjoys all the advantages his class affords him. He remains loyal to Mickey, telling him “You’re still my best friend,” but his naïveté about class differences is a flaw. His line “I don’t care about money” shows he does not understand what it means to have none. His affair with Linda is the final trigger for the tragedy.

As children, Mickey and Edward are similar — playful, curious, and drawn to each other. They think each other is good-looking and will easily find girlfriends. But as adults, their paths diverge completely. Mickey faces factory work, unemployment, crime, and prison. Edward enjoys university, a career in politics, and financial security. Russell uses their parallel lives to argue that it is nurture, not nature, that determines a person’s future.

Mrs Johnstone

Mrs Johnstone is the biological mother of the twins. She is warm, loving, and fun, but trapped by poverty. She cannot afford to keep both babies and is manipulated by Mrs Lyons into giving Edward away. Her line “I can’t afford to keep both of them” reveals the impossible situation she faces.

Despite her hardship, Mrs Johnstone has a strong sense of fun and optimism. She sings, jokes, and comforts her children. As she ages, she carries the guilt of the secret. Her line “I’ll always love you, Mickey” shows deep maternal affection. In the final scene, she reveals the truth — “I had to give one away” — which triggers the fatal confrontation. She represents the working class: generous, resilient, but crushed by a system that gives her no choices.

Key Fact

Mrs Johnstone’s key quotes: “I can’t afford to keep both of them” shows her desperation and poverty. “I’ll always love you, Mickey” shows deep maternal affection. “I had to give one away” is the tragic revelation that triggers the climax.
Voice: Warm, melodic tone with a Liverpool accent. Pace quickens when anxious.
Physicality: Open, expressive gestures showing warmth. As she ages, posture becomes more stooped, movements slower, showing the weight of her secret.

Mrs Lyons

Mrs Lyons is Edward’s adoptive mother and Mrs Johnstone’s employer. She is initially presented as lonely and desperate for a child. She manipulates Mrs Johnstone by using a Bible oath to keep the secret, saying “You swore on the Bible.”

As the play progresses, Mrs Lyons becomes increasingly paranoid, possessive, and unstable. She fires Mrs Johnstone, saying “I think you should go,” out of fear that Mrs Johnstone will become too attached to Edward. Her jealousy erupts — “You don’t own him!” She eventually attempts to stab Mrs Johnstone. Her decline from respectable middle-class woman to violent, mentally unstable figure shows how guilt and deception destroy from within.

Key Fact

Mrs Lyons says “He’s mine!” — her possessiveness spirals into fear and instability. Compare this with Mrs Johnstone’s selfless love. Russell uses these two mothers to contrast wealth with warmth, and control with care.

Mr Lyons

Mr Lyons is Edward’s adoptive father and a factory owner. He represents the capitalist upper class. He is largely absent from family life, prioritising work over relationships. His most significant action is making his workforce redundant, which directly causes Mickey’s unemployment. He embodies the theme of class power — the decisions of the wealthy have devastating consequences for the working class.

Key Fact

Mr Lyons represents the absent father and capitalist power. His most significant action — making his workforce redundant — directly causes Mickey’s unemployment.
Voice: Formal RP accent, measured pace, authoritative tone. Detached when delivering bad news.
Physicality: Upright, confident posture. Minimal gestures — controlled and business-like. Uses elevated positions (behind desks) to show power over the working class.

Linda

Linda grows up alongside Mickey and Edward. As a child, she is bright, positive, and enthusiastic. She defends Mickey — “Leave him alone!” — and is a loyal friend to both boys. She eventually marries Mickey, telling him “I love you, Mickey.”

As an adult, Linda watches Mickey deteriorate after prison. Her key line — “You’re not the Mickey I married” — highlights his decline. Desperate and lonely, she begins an affair with Edward. Linda is not portrayed as a villain; Russell presents her sympathetically as someone trapped by circumstances, just as Mrs Johnstone was.

Key Fact

Linda’s key quotes: “Leave him alone!” (as a child — shows loyalty and courage), “I love you, Mickey” (shows genuine affection), “You’re not the Mickey I married” (shows heartbreak at his decline).
Voice: As a child — bright, energetic, higher pitch. As an adult — lower pitch, wearier tone, quieter volume reflecting exhaustion.
Physicality: As a child — animated, open body language, quick movements. As an adult — slower, more closed, carrying the weight of responsibility.

Sammy

Sammy is Mickey’s older brother and a product of the same deprived environment. He is rebellious from childhood, getting into trouble at school and later burning part of the school down. As an adult, Sammy is involved in serious crime. His line “Come on, Mickey, just do it” pressures Mickey into the robbery that destroys his life. Sammy wears dark colours as an adult to show he lives a criminal lifestyle and needs to keep to the shadows. He represents how poverty and lack of opportunity can push people toward crime.

Key Fact

Sammy’s key quote: “Come on, Mickey, just do it” — he pressures Mickey into the robbery that destroys his life.
Voice: Aggressive tone, louder volume, Liverpool accent broader than Mickey’s to show he is rougher and more streetwise.
Physicality: Swagger, wide stance, uses space aggressively. As an adult — furtive movements, looking over his shoulder, keeping to the shadows. Dark clothing reinforces his criminal lifestyle.

The Narrator

The Narrator is not a traditional character but a dramatic device. He exists outside the story, commenting on the action and addressing the audience directly. He foreshadows events, creates dramatic irony, and represents fate itself. His lines — “The devil’s got your number” and “Shoes upon the table” — are recurring warnings of the tragedy to come. He is anonymous and controlling, which is why he is the only character who could justifiably wear a mask.

Key Fact

The Narrator’s key quotes: “The devil’s got your number” and “Shoes upon the table” — recurring warnings of tragedy. He is the only character who could justifiably wear a mask, as he represents fate itself.
Voice: Deep, authoritative tone. Measured, deliberate pace. Uses direct address to break the fourth wall.
Physicality: Controlled and still. Stands apart from other characters. Minimal gestures — his power comes from words and presence, not physical action.

All other characters in Blood Brothers — the milkman, the policeman, the neighbours, the children at school — are played by the ensemble. These actors multi-role, using changes in costume, voice, and physicality to distinguish between characters. The ensemble creates the world of the play, representing the community around the main characters.

Key Scenes for Character

When revising characters, focus on these key scenes that reveal character development:

Mrs Johnstone agrees to give her baby away — shows her desperation and Mrs Lyons’ manipulation. Mickey and Edward become friends — shows childhood innocence before class divides them. Mrs Johnstone gives Edward the locket — shows her continuing love for both sons. Mickey in prison — shows his total breakdown. The final scene — all character arcs converge in tragedy.

practice_questions.text: As a costume designer, describe the costumes you would use for Mickey as a child and as an adult to reflect his changing circumstances.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed description of both costumes with clear justification linked to character and class. E.g. As a child, Mickey would wear grey shorts with visible darned patches, a home-knitted jumper, and scuffed leather shoes to show his working-class background and poverty. As an adult, he would wear faded jeans, a worn denim jacket, and a faded red t-shirt to show he is still poor and his clothing is well-worn. The fading reflects his emotional decline.
Lower band (1-2): Basic description with limited justification. E.g. He would wear old clothes as a child and jeans as an adult.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an actor playing Mrs Lyons might use vocal skills to deliver the line: “You swore on the Bible.”
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of vocal techniques with clear effect. E.g. Mrs Lyons could use a sharp, accusatory tone to show she is using guilt as a weapon. She might emphasise the word ‘Bible’ with increased volume and a pause before it to give it weight and remind Mrs Johnstone of the seriousness of her oath. A measured, controlled pace would show her manipulative nature — she is calculated, not emotional. A clipped, RP accent would reinforce her middle-class authority.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to one vocal skill. E.g. She would say it loudly to show she is angry.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an actor playing Edward as a child might use physicality to show his loneliness when he first approaches Mickey.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of physical skills with justified effect. E.g. Edward could use hesitant, small steps with a slow gait to show he is unsure about approaching Mickey. He might hold his hands together in front of his body, suggesting shyness and a lack of social confidence. When Mickey responds positively, Edward’s posture could open up — shoulders back, wide smile, eager eye contact — showing genuine happiness at making his first real friend. This contrast in physicality communicates his emotional transformation to the audience.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to physicality. E.g. He would look shy and then happy.

practice_questions.text: Choose a main character whose appearance changes in Blood Brothers. Explain how you would use costume, hair, makeup or masks to show the change of appearance for this character in two scenes/sections from the performance text.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how costume/hair/makeup changes communicate character development across two scenes. Detailed semiotic analysis.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation with some relevant detail across two scenes.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with basic reference to appearance change.
E.g. Mickey: As a child — grey shorts with patches, scuffed shoes, home-knitted red jumper (poverty, innocence). As an adult after prison — faded, oversized clothes hanging off a thinner frame, unwashed hair, pale makeup with dark circles under eyes (depression, defeat, the toll of prison and medication). The contrast shows the audience how circumstances have destroyed Mickey.

practice_questions.text: Choose one character from Blood Brothers. As an actor, explain how you would prepare to perform this character for one scene/section of the performance text.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of preparation covering research (context, playwright’s intentions), vocal and physical choices, character development, and rehearsal techniques.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation of preparation with some relevant detail.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with basic reference to preparation.
Preparation might include: reading the script closely, researching the social/historical context, analysing the character’s journey, developing a backstory, experimenting with vocal delivery and physicality, working with other actors on proxemics and relationships.

practice_questions.text: Select the character Mickey from Blood Brothers. Describe the vocal and physical skills an actor playing Mickey could use to show emotion in one key moment. Give examples from the performance text to justify your response.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how an actor would communicate emotion in a key moment. Accomplished understanding of physical and vocal skills to convey meaning with relevant examples from the text.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation of emotion. Clear understanding of physical and vocal skills with some justification and examples.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation of emotion and use of physical/vocal skills. Limited understanding with few examples.
Focus is on vocal and physical skills: voice, mime, non-verbal communication, facial expression, proxemics, use of levels.

before.content_html:
Overview

To succeed in the exam, you need to understand not just what happens in Blood Brothers, but why Willy Russell wrote it. The play is deeply rooted in the social, historical, and cultural context of 1980s Liverpool. Russell uses his characters and their situations to comment on class inequality, the impact of government policy, and the way society treats its poorest members.

Social Context

Social context in Blood Brothers is shown through how characters relate to each other and how society judges them. The Johnstone family is looked down on by those around them. When they find out the Johnstones are moving to their area, neighbours gather together in disapproval. The police officer treats the Johnstone and Lyons families completely differently — harsh and threatening to the working class, polite and apologetic to the middle class.

Mr Lyons makes his entire workforce unemployed, showing how the decisions of the wealthy have devastating consequences for ordinary people. The bailiffs repossess Mrs Johnstone’s property — items bought from the catalogue — showing how catalogue debt trapped working-class families in cycles of poverty.

Key Fact

The police officer scene is a powerful example of class bias. The same children doing the same thing are treated completely differently based on their family’s social class. Russell uses this to show the audience that the system is rigged against the poor.

Historical Context

Blood Brothers was written in 1981 and is set from the late 1950s to the early 1980s. Understanding what was happening in Britain during this period is essential for exam answers about context.

1979

Margaret Thatcher Becomes Prime Minister

Thatcher led the Conservative government that pushed to move away from manual labour and heavy industry. Factory closures left thousands unemployed.

1981

Toxteth Riots

Riots broke out in the Toxteth area of Liverpool, driven by unemployment, poverty, and frustration with police treatment of working-class communities. The government sent a minister to Merseyside to run regeneration projects, but many people in Liverpool felt the help was too small and came too late.

1980s

Welfare Changes & Mass Unemployment

Changes to the welfare system and a huge increase in people on the dole hit communities like the Johnstones hard. Stricter punishments for crime meant people like Mickey faced severe consequences with little support for rehabilitation.

Russell’s themes remain relevant today. There are still high levels of unemployment in parts of the UK. Children still grow up in poverty. The gap between rich and poor continues to widen. The play asks its audience: has anything really changed? A director staging Blood Brothers today would want the audience to recognise these same issues in their own communities.

Cultural Context

Cultural context in Blood Brothers reflects what people did for fun and pleasure in the era the play is set. Russell uses cultural details to ground the play in a specific time and place.

Going to the cinema: As teenagers, Mickey and Edward go to the cinema to watch “saucy” films, showing their growing interest in the opposite sex. The cinema was a common, affordable form of entertainment. Playing on the streets: As children, Mickey, Edward, and Linda play outside, which was the norm before video games and social media. Marilyn Monroe: Mrs Johnstone sings about Marilyn Monroe, the film star she was compared to when she was young. Russell brings the song back later, when her life is much harder. The reference fixes the play in the 1950s and 1960s and tracks how her hopes fade.

Themes

Blood Brothers explores seven major themes. Each one can be linked to specific characters, scenes, and context.

Social class is the central theme. The twins are genetically identical but raised in opposite classes. Mickey grows up in poverty with limited education and opportunities. Edward grows up wealthy with access to the best schools and a secure future. Russell argues that class — not talent or character — determines life outcomes. The police officer, the teachers, and even neighbours treat the two families differently based on class alone.

Are we shaped by our genes or our environment? Mickey and Edward are the perfect test case — same DNA, different upbringings, completely different outcomes. Russell’s conclusion is clear: nurture wins. It is the environment, not the person, that creates criminals, addicts, and failures. Mickey’s line “I could have been him!” drives this point home.

Fate runs through the play from the cyclical structure to the Narrator’s warnings. The superstition of “shoes upon the table” and the recurring image of the magpie suggest that the twins’ deaths were always destined to happen. However, Russell leaves the audience with a question: was it really fate, or was it the class system that killed them?

Key Fact

Russell deliberately sets up a tension between fate and class as explanations for the tragedy. The Narrator suggests superstition and destiny are to blame. But the events of the play suggest it is poverty, inequality, and a broken system. This ambiguity makes the play powerful — the audience must decide for themselves.

Other Key Themes

Education: Edward receives an excellent education that opens doors. Mickey’s education is poor, and he leaves school without qualifications. Russell shows education as a tool that reinforces class division rather than breaking it.

Growing up: The play traces the characters from innocent children to burdened adults. The songs and Narrator mark the passage of time, showing how life choices narrow as the characters age. Childhood play gives way to adult responsibility, crime, and heartbreak.

Men and women: Women in the play — Mrs Johnstone, Mrs Lyons, and Linda — are all trapped by circumstances beyond their control. Mrs Johnstone is abandoned by her husband and left to raise children alone. Linda is pressured into choices by Mickey’s decline. Russell highlights how women in working-class communities bore the heaviest burdens.

Money: Money determines everything in Blood Brothers. It determines where you live, how you are treated by the police, whether you go to university, and ultimately whether you live or die. Edward’s naïve line “I don’t care about money” only makes sense because he has always had it.

Locations & What They Represent

Russell uses locations to reinforce the class divide visually and aurally on stage.

Liverpool City Centre (Johnstone family): Poor people lived near industrial areas and the docklands, which were bombed in the Second World War. Housing was poor quality and bomb-damaged. A director could use sounds of industry to create this environment. Urban Liverpool (Lyons family): Richer people lived in larger houses away from the docklands. A director could use birdsong and quiet to create a sense of peace and privilege. Skelmersdale: When the Johnstones are relocated, they move to a quieter area with birdsong and occasional car sounds — a brief moment of hope before things unravel again.

practice_questions.text: As a costume designer, describe the costumes you would use for the Johnstone and Lyons families to communicate the social class divide to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed description of contrasting costumes with clear justification linked to class. E.g. The Johnstones would wear home-knitted, patched, and well-worn clothing in muted colours to show poverty. Mrs Johnstone’s wide-skirted dress and flat shoes show she is practical and cannot afford luxuries. The Lyons family would wear well-tailored suits, polished shoes, and high-quality materials to show wealth. Mrs Lyons’ high heels show she does not have to do physical work. The colour contrast (red for Johnstone/Labour vs blue for Lyons/Conservative) would communicate political affiliations.
Lower band (1-2): Basic description with limited justification. E.g. Poor family in old clothes, rich family in nice clothes.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an actor playing Mrs Johnstone might use vocal skills to deliver the line: “I can’t afford to keep both of them.”
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of vocal techniques with clear effect. E.g. The actor could use a trembling, quiet volume to show the emotional weight of admitting she cannot provide for her children. A slow pace with pauses would communicate her reluctance and pain. Emphasis on ‘can’t’ would highlight her helplessness — she has no choice. A Liverpool accent would ground her in the working-class community and remind the audience of the social context. Her tone could crack on ‘both’ to show she loves both children equally.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to one vocal skill. E.g. She would speak sadly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an actor playing the Narrator might use physicality in a scene where he warns the audience about fate, to create tension.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of physical skills with justified effect. E.g. The Narrator could use a slow, deliberate gait to cross the stage, suggesting he is in no rush because fate is inevitable. Strong, upright posture with controlled gestures would communicate authority and control. He might make direct eye contact with the audience to break the fourth wall and make them complicit in the knowledge of what is coming. Tight, restrained muscle tension would contrast with the other characters’ emotional turmoil, showing his detachment.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to physicality. E.g. He would walk around the stage looking serious.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer could show historical and/or cultural context at one key moment in Blood Brothers. As part of your answer, roughly sketch an annotated design to help explain the layout of the set.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how set design communicates historical/cultural context. E.g. For the Skelmersdale relocation scene, the set could show a 1970s council estate with a playground, small gardens, and a bus stop — reflecting the real overspill estates built to move Liverpool families out of the slums. Faded red brick flats on the backdrop communicate working-class housing. Cultural context shown through a corner shop with period-appropriate signage and a milk float.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation with some historical/cultural detail.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with little or no contextual understanding.

practice_questions.text: As a sound designer, explain three sound effects you would use to show the social, historical or cultural context of Blood Brothers. Give examples from the performance text to justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identified sound effect, to a maximum of 3 marks. 1 mark for linking to social/historical/cultural context, to a maximum of 3 marks.

Sound effects should demonstrate understanding of context.
• Factory machinery sounds — historical context of industrial Liverpool in the 1960s–70s.
• Beatles music playing on a radio — cultural context of 1960s Liverpool.
• Children playing in the street — social context of working-class neighbourhood life.
• Dole queue ambience / crowd murmuring — historical context of mass unemployment under Thatcher.
• Church bells — cultural/religious context of Catholic working-class Liverpool.

practice_questions.text: As a director, identify the mood you want to communicate for one key moment in Blood Brothers. You must not use the closing scene/section. Explain how you would create the mood.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how to create a specific mood using a range of directorial tools (blocking, pace, actor direction, design elements). Effective examples from the text.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation with some relevant examples.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with basic reference to mood.
The mood must be identified and linked to a specific moment. The director should consider: how actors deliver lines, blocking and proxemics, lighting, sound, set, and costume choices.

before.content_html:
Performance Skills in the Exam

In Section A of your written drama exam, you will be asked how an actor would use voice and physicality to communicate meaning. You need to know the specific terminology for each skill and be able to apply it to characters and moments in Blood Brothers. You also need to understand semiotics — how signs and symbols on stage create meaning for the audience.

Voice Skills

There are eight voice skills to know:

Key Fact — Voice Skills

Clarity — how clearly the actor speaks so the audience can understand every word. Tone — the emotional quality of the voice (e.g. warm, cold, sarcastic, desperate). Pace — how fast or slow the actor speaks. Pitch — how high or low the voice is. Accent — the regional or social way of speaking (e.g. a Liverpool accent for Mickey, Received Pronunciation for Edward). Pause — a deliberate silence for dramatic effect. Volume — how loud or quiet the actor speaks. Emphasis — stress placed on a specific word to change meaning.

How voice changes between characters and between Acts:

  • Edward (child): Received Pronunciation (RP) accent to show his wealthy background. Enthusiastic tone, fast pace, and clear voice to show confidence and eagerness when meeting Mickey.
  • Mickey (child): Liverpool accent reflecting his working-class Liverpool roots. Louder volume and faster pace to show energy and streetwise confidence.
  • Mickey (adult, post-prison): Quiet volume, slow pace, flat tone to show his depression. Emphasis on “him” when saying “I could have been him!” to communicate envy and resentment.
  • Mrs Lyons (Act Two): Higher pitch, faster pace, more strained tone to show her increasing paranoia and instability.
  • The Narrator: Controlled pace, low pitch, sinister tone. Deliberate pauses before key words to build tension. Clear and measured delivery to maintain authority.

Physicality Skills

Use the mnemonic “Head Shoulders Knees and Toes” (thinking about the whole body) to remember that physicality covers everything from head to toe. The key terms are:

Key Fact — Physicality Skills

Eye contact — who the character looks at and when. Facial expression — what the face communicates (joy, fear, anger). Posture — how the character holds their body (upright, slumped, tense). Muscle tension — how tight or relaxed the body is. Gesture — specific hand or arm movements to communicate meaning. Body language — overall physical communication (open, closed, defensive). Gait — how the character walks (confident stride, shuffling, hurried). Levels — whether the character is standing, sitting, crouching, or elevated. Proximity — the distance between characters on stage.

How physicality changes between characters and between Acts:

  • Edward (child): Open body language showing sincerity. Upright posture showing confidence. Happy facial expressions, enthusiastic gestures. Moves towards Mickey (close proximity) to show eagerness.
  • Mickey (child): Energetic gait, animated gestures, relaxed muscle tension. Wide stance and confident posture despite his poverty — he is streetwise and bold.
  • Mickey (adult, post-prison): Slumped posture, shuffling gait, minimal gestures, high muscle tension. Avoids eye contact. Keeps a bigger distance from other characters. Low levels — he may sit or hunch while others stand.
  • Mrs Lyons (Act One): Upright posture, controlled gestures, tight body language. In Act Two, she becomes physically erratic — wild gestures, pacing, invading Mrs Johnstone’s space.
  • The Narrator: Controlled, deliberate movements. Often positioned at a higher level or on the periphery of the action, watching. Still posture that contrasts with the emotional chaos of other characters.

Semiotics — Creating Meaning on Stage

Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols. In drama, everything on stage is a sign that communicates meaning to the audience — from the colour of a costume to the direction of a spotlight. Russell uses semiotics throughout Blood Brothers:

  • Colour symbolism — Mickey’s red jumper links to the Labour Party and working-class identity; Edward’s blue links to the Conservative Party and wealth
  • Set symbolism — doors, levels, and the use of the stage floor all communicate status and access
  • Sound symbolism — the singular magpie cackle represents sorrow; the heartbeat represents stress
  • Proxemics — characters move closer to the audience when they want empathy, and further away when they know what they are doing is wrong
  • Lighting symbolism — colour washes, gobos, and spotlights all carry meaning beyond simply illuminating the stage
  • Costume symbolism — fabric quality, colour, and condition all signal class, mood, and character arc

The COSTUMES Acronym

For any design question in the exam, use the COSTUMES acronym to structure your answer. This works for costume, set, lighting, and sound questions:

Key Fact — The COSTUMES Framework

Context — what is the character’s situation? Opinion — in my opinion, I would… Style — what is the style of the production? Time Period — when is the play set? Uber (location) — where is the scene taking place? Materials — what materials, fabrics, or equipment would be used? Examples from the text — reference a specific moment. Semiotics — what meaning does your choice communicate to the audience?

Stage Directions

Stage directions are written instructions for actors and designers. In Blood Brothers, they serve three purposes:

  • Practical information — whether a character is singing or speaking
  • Motivation — for example, “a satisfied smile by Linda” implies she was pleased to impress Mickey when shooting the air pistol
  • Emotion — for example, “Mrs Johnstone runs frantically” tells us about her state of mind

In the exam, you can use stage directions as evidence. If asked how an actor would perform a scene, the stage directions give you Russell’s intended emotions and motivations, which you can then translate into specific voice and physicality choices.

Proxemics — the use of distance on stage — is one of the most powerful tools an actor has. In Blood Brothers:

  • Close proximity — Mickey and Edward stand close when they first become friends, showing their instant bond. Mrs Lyons invades Mrs Johnstone’s space to show manipulation and control.
  • Distance — Mickey moves away from Linda and Edward in Act Two, showing emotional withdrawal. Mrs Johnstone stands far from Mrs Lyons when she knows the secret is dangerous.
  • Proximity to the audience — the Narrator moves close to the audience when foreshadowing events, breaking the fourth wall. Mrs Johnstone comes to the apron for “Tell Me It’s Not True,” drawing the audience into her grief.

In the exam, you may be given a specific line and asked how an actor would deliver it. Follow this structure:

Example: Edward says “Do you want to be my friend?”

  • Accent: RP accent to show Edward comes from a wealthy background.
  • Tone: Enthusiastic tone to show he is lonely and genuinely wants to make friends.
  • Clarity: Clear voice to show he is a confident young man.
  • Body language: Open body language to show sincerity.
  • Facial expression: Happy facial expressions to show excitement about making a new friend.

Notice how each point names the skill, describes how it would be used, and explains why — what it tells the audience about the character.

The Director’s Role

In your written drama exam, you may be asked how a director would stage a specific scene from Blood Brothers. To answer well, you need to understand what a director actually does and how they bring a scene to life through decisions about performance, design, and dramatic conventions.

Key Fact — What a Director Does

A director is responsible for the overall artistic vision of the production. They work with actors and the creative team (including lighting, sound, set, and costume designers). They lead rehearsals, guide actors on interpretation, give notes to improve the work, and agree blocking (the planned movement of actors on stage).

Key Scenes You Must Know

The exam may ask about any moment in the play, but these are the most important scenes that you should be able to analyse in detail. For each one, you need to explain how a director would use performance skills, design elements, and dramatic conventions to communicate meaning.

This is the catalyst for the entire play. Mrs Lyons persuades Mrs Johnstone to give away one of her unborn twins, and Mrs Johnstone swears on the Bible.

  • Voice: Mrs Lyons would use a calm, persuasive tone with measured pace to show she is in control. Mrs Johnstone would use a hesitant tone, quiet volume, and frequent pauses to show she is unsure but feels she has no choice.
  • Physicality: Mrs Lyons should lean towards Mrs Johnstone (close proximity) to show manipulation. Mrs Johnstone would shrink away — slumped posture, avoiding eye contact, hands wringing (high muscle tension).
  • Lighting: A red strobe pulsating from 100% to 50% intensity when Mrs Johnstone swears on the Bible to symbolise this is a dangerous decision.
  • Sound: A non-diegetic heartbeat to show Mrs Johnstone’s stress, combined with a singular magpie cackle to foreshadow sorrow.
  • This is a marking the moment — the director should ensure the audience understands that this oath is the catalyst for every tragedy that follows.

The twins meet by chance at age seven and immediately bond. Edward asks “Do you want to be my friend?” and they make a pact to become blood brothers — not knowing they are real brothers.

  • Voice: Edward speaks with an RP accent (wealthy background), enthusiastic tone, and clear voice showing confidence. Mickey speaks with a Scouse accent, faster pace, and louder volume showing energy and streetwise character.
  • Physicality: Both boys use open body language, excited facial expressions, and animated gestures. They start at a distance and gradually move closer as friendship develops, ending in close proximity for the blood brothers pact.
  • Lighting: Warm straw wash to show happiness and innocence. Bright intensity to reflect the joy of childhood.
  • Dramatic irony: The audience knows the boys are real brothers, making this scene both joyful and heartbreaking.
  • Marking the moment: The blood brothers pact is the second catalyst — the director should slow the pace and focus the audience’s attention on this symbolic act.

Other children bully Mickey, highlighting his vulnerability and the class divide that is already present even in childhood.

  • Physicality: The bullying children should use high levels (standing over Mickey) and close, intimidating proximity. Mickey should use defensive body language — crossed arms, lowered levels, tension in his shoulders.
  • Voice: The children use mocking tones and loud volume. Mickey’s responses should show a mix of defiance (volume, emphasis) and hurt (quieter moments, pauses).
  • Lighting: A crossfade from warm straw to cold steel wash would show the shift from happiness to Mickey’s unhappiness.

Mrs Johnstone gives Edward a locket with a photograph of herself and Mickey inside, as a secret connection to his real family. Seven years later, when the boys are in their mid-teens, Mrs Lyons discovers the locket. By this point she is consumed with paranoia about losing Edward, and she attempts to stab Mrs Johnstone with a kitchen knife.

  • Voice: Mrs Lyons’ voice should shift from a controlled, cold tone (when she first sees the locket) to a high-pitched, fast-paced, screaming delivery as her paranoia erupts. Mrs Johnstone’s voice should show shock — gasping, raised volume, pleading tone.
  • Physicality: Mrs Lyons grabs the knife with a violent gesture. Her body should show high muscle tension, erratic movements, and wild facial expressions. Mrs Johnstone should physically retreat, using the stage space to show her fear (backing away towards the audience).
  • Sound: A sharp, discordant non-diegetic sound effect at the moment of the stabbing attempt. Silence immediately after to let the horror sink in.

After being drawn into crime through Sammy, Mickey is imprisoned for seven years. When released, he is dependent on antidepressants. Linda hides his medication, trying to help him move on, but this only increases his desperation.

  • Set: Two uncomfortable chairs and a prison bar gobo to create a cold, stark environment.
  • Voice (Mickey in prison): Flat tone, low volume, slow pace, long pauses. His voice should sound empty — the energy and defiance of his youth have completely gone.
  • Physicality (Mickey in prison): Slumped posture, shuffling gait, minimal gestures, avoiding eye contact. He sits at a low level while Linda stands, showing the reversal of their childhood dynamic.
  • Physicality (Linda hiding pills): Secretive body language — glancing over her shoulder, quick hand movements, facial expression showing a mix of worry and determination.

The Final Scene

The final scene is the most important in the play. Mrs Lyons tells Mickey that Linda and Edward have been seeing each other. Mickey takes Sammy’s gun and confronts Edward at the Town Hall. Mrs Johnstone runs in and tells them they are twins. Mickey, distraught (“I could have been him!”), fires the gun by accident and kills Edward. The police then shoot Mickey. Mrs Johnstone is left with both sons dead.

Key Fact — Staging the Final Scene

A director staging the final scene would consider: blocking — Mickey and Edward should be centre stage, with the ensemble and police forming a surrounding group. Mrs Johnstone could be on the apron, closest to the audience. Levels — Edward might be elevated (on a stage or behind a lectern in the Town Hall), while Mickey is at ground level, looking up. This physically shows the class divide one final time. Lighting — a white spotlight on Mrs Johnstone singing “Tell Me It’s Not True,” isolating her grief. Blue and red pulsating strobes from stage left to show the police have arrived. Sound — the gunshot, then silence, then Mrs Johnstone’s song. The orchestra should be still during the gunshot to let the sound land with full impact.

Dramatic Conventions

Russell uses several dramatic conventions throughout Blood Brothers. You must be able to identify these and explain their effect:

  • Dramatic irony — the audience knows Mickey and Edward are real brothers; the characters do not. This makes every moment of their friendship more poignant.
  • Narrator fills gaps — the Narrator explains events that happen off-stage, such as how the teenagers grow up. He controls the pace and the audience’s knowledge.
  • Passage of time — the play covers approximately 25 years. The director must find ways to show ageing through costume, voice, physicality, and staging changes.
  • Cross-cutting — when Linda and Edward kiss while Mrs Lyons shows Mickey, two storylines are presented at the same time to build tension.
  • Marking the moment — two key moments are “marked”: the Bible oath (catalyst one) and the blood brothers pact (catalyst two). The director slows the action and focuses the audience’s attention.
  • Duologue — a scene between two characters, such as when Mrs Lyons explains to Mrs Johnstone that she cannot have children.
  • Monologue — a scene where one character speaks alone, such as when Mickey realises Edward is his twin and that he could have had Edward’s life.

Two contrasting scenes that show the class divide in action:

  • Mr Lyons makes staff redundant: The director should position Mr Lyons elevated (behind a desk or lectern) with the workers at a lower level looking up. This blocking physically communicates the power imbalance. Mr Lyons’ voice should be formal and detached — he does not understand the impact of his decision on working-class families like the Johnstones.
  • Mickey asks Linda out: This scene should contrast with the redundancy scene. Mickey is nervous — hesitant voice, quiet volume, fidgeting gestures, avoiding eye contact. Linda should respond with warmth — smiling facial expression, open body language, moving closer (reducing proximity). A warm lighting wash supports the positive mood.
  • Edward is frozen out: During this scene, Edward is present but gradually excluded. He stands apart, watching Mickey and Linda together. He exits quietly, which is the first suggestion to the audience that Edward is in love with Linda but respects Mickey too much to intervene. A director should use a subtle lighting fade on Edward as Mickey and Linda draw closer together.
Key Fact — Marking the Moment

Marking the moment is when the director deliberately highlights a crucial point in the play to make the audience pay special attention. In Blood Brothers, the two moments that are “marked” are: (1) Mrs Johnstone swearing on the Bible — the catalyst that sets the whole tragedy in motion, and (2) Mickey and Edward making their blood brothers pact — the catalyst that bonds the twins and makes the eventual tragedy even more devastating. A director might use a freeze, a lighting change, a sound effect, or a slowing of pace to mark these moments.
